title: Max Consecutive Ones III — sliding window allowing at most K zero flips.
shortTitle: Max Consecutive Ones III — Sliding Window Allowing At Most K Zero Flips

s1_definition.profdef: Max Consecutive Ones III finds the longest run of consecutive 1s obtainable in a binary array if you may flip at most K zeros to ones. A variable-size sliding window grows the right edge, counting zeros inside the window; when the zero count exceeds K the left edge shrinks until at most K zeros remain, and the largest window seen is the answer. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a daily uptime string where 1 means a service was up and 0 means down, and it may excuse at most K down-days as maintenance. Rajesh finds the longest stretch of "up" days he can claim if he is allowed to recolor at most K down-days as up, growing a window and shrinking it whenever it contains too many excused downs.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a window counting zeros; keep it valid while zeros are at most K, and the widest such window is the answer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Max Consecutive Ones III finds the longest run of consecutive 1s obtainable in a binary array if you may flip at most K zeros to ones. A variable-size sliding window grows the right edge, counting zeros inside the window; when the zero count exceeds K the left edge shrinks until at most K zeros remain, and the largest window seen is the answer. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a daily uptime string where 1 means a service was up and 0 means down, and it may excuse at most K down-days as maintenance. Rajesh finds the longest stretch of "up" days he can claim if he is allowed to recolor at most K down-days as up, growing a window and shrinking it whenever it contains too many excused downs.

**One line to remember:** Slide a window counting zeros; keep it valid while zeros are at most K, and the widest such window is the answer.

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain `left = 0`, a `zeros` counter, and `best = 0`. For each `right`, if `a[right] == 0` increment `zeros`. Then, while `zeros > k`, if `a[left] == 0` decrement `zeros`, and advance `left`. After restoring validity, update `best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1)`. The window width always represents a run of 1s achievable by flipping at most K of its zeros.

A code snippet on the uptime array: `int longestOnes(int[] a, int k) { int l=0, zeros=0, best=0; for (int r=0; r<a.length; r++) { if (a[r]==0) zeros++; while (zeros > k) { if (a[l]==0) zeros--; l++; } best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1); } return best; }`. There is no need to physically flip anything; counting the zeros inside the window is enough because any window with at most K zeros can be turned into all ones by flipping them.

A slight variation keeps the left pointer moving without a nested loop by only advancing it one step when the zero budget is exceeded, which makes the window non-shrinking and returns the final window width. Both are linear; the explicit shrink version is clearer for explaining the invariant.

A senior nuance is that this is the general form of several problems: setting K to zero gives the plain longest run of ones, and the same window structure solves "longest substring with at most K of some character replaced." The invariant is simply that the window never contains more zeros than the flip budget, and because each pointer only moves forward it is linear despite the inner loop.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India service-level team records daily uptime as a binary string and may excuse up to K down-days as planned maintenance when computing the longest continuous availability stretch for an SLA report. This is exactly how Max Consecutive Ones III works — flip at most K zeros and find the longest run.

Problem 2 — The uptime history is long, so an O(n) window is required rather than trying every stretch.

The code shows an `UptimeAnalyzer` with `longestAvailability`, a demo on an uptime array, and the longest excusable availability run.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: uptime [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1], K is 2.

Step 1: Right expands over 1, 1 (zeros 0), then 0 (zeros 1), then 0 (zeros 2), all within K 2. Window is indexes 0 to 3, width 4, best 4.

Step 2: Right adds 1 at index 4 (zeros still 2), width 5, best 5. Adds 1 at 5, width 6, best 6. Adds 1 at 6, width 7, best 7. The window now spans indexes 0 to 6 with two excused zeros.

Step 3: Right adds 0 at index 7, zeros becomes 3, exceeding K 2, so shrink. The left pointer advances, and when it passes the first zero at index 2, zeros drops to 2; left is now at index 3.

Step 4: The window is indexes 3 to 7, width 5, with two zeros (at 3 and 7), best stays 7. Right adds 1 at index 8, zeros stays 2, width 6, best stays 7.

Step 5: The scan ends with best 7, the longest stretch of up-days achievable by excusing two down-days, which was indexes 0 to 6. The method returns 7.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Longest availability run with 2 excused: 7
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Max Consecutive Ones III asks for the longest run of ones I can achieve in a binary array if I may flip at most K zeros, and it is a clean variable-size sliding window. I grow the right edge and count the zeros inside the window. As long as the zero count is within the flip budget the window is valid, and whenever a new zero pushes the count above K, I shrink from the left until the window contains at most K zeros again. The widest window I ever hold is the answer.

The insight that makes this simple is that I never actually flip anything. Any window containing at most K zeros can be turned into an unbroken run of ones by flipping exactly those zeros, so counting them is all I need, and the window width directly equals the achievable run length. That reframing turns a flipping problem into a plain zero-counting window.

This structure is more general than it looks. Setting the budget to zero gives the ordinary longest run of ones, and the exact same window solves the longest substring with at most K of some character replaced. The invariant is just that the window never holds more zeros than the budget, and because both pointers only move forward the algorithm is linear even with the inner shrink loop.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the service-level team's reporting. Daily uptime was recorded as a binary string, and the SLA rules allowed excusing up to K down-days as planned maintenance when computing the longest continuous availability stretch, so the flip budget mapped directly onto excused outages. With a long uptime history the linear window was essential rather than testing every stretch. Explaining the zero-counting window, the no-actual-flip insight, and the generality of the pattern shows the interviewer I understand the problem beyond memorizing the loop.

keyPoints: Fixed window: max sum of K consecutive elements
Variable window: longest substring without repeating
Expand right, shrink left based on condition
Track window state with HashMap or array
